## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Andreas and Ingrid both say too few calls are lost to pay for, so the group is right and plainly named; Karim (doesn't know his missed share, wants a free test) and Hannes (won't pay at any price because guests won't talk to a robot) make different points and rightly stand on their own.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line: all four speak to what the tool would be worth, Hannes's refusal included.

founder.order_why: The flow runs context, problem, idea, buyer, then sending, which fits how I'd pitch Codyco, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) comes after I had already set my first step as the €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel (20-21), so it reads like an afterthought instead of part of the commitment step.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 (the same context question shown twice); screen 22 'Offer a pilot?' repeats what screens 20-21 already captured (the paid money-back pilot); screens 14 and 17 overlap, since the owner's agreement and the data protection review both read as what has to clear before the group pays.
founder.missing: Nothing asked how my price is shaped: a per-hotel monthly licence after an up-front pilot fee that is money-back and credited on roll-out. A single price box can't hold both. Nothing asked how many hotels a group runs, and the roll-out across the group is where the money is. Nothing asked whether the group has a central reservations office or call center already answering after hours, which decides whether the 5% applies at all.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The flow from lost calls to price, budget, sign-off, data protection and the pilot makes sense, but the 'One more thing' screen lands between 5 of 6 and 6 of 6 and briefly felt like the study was ending before the pilot question came.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 6 and 7 overlap: I had just given the time for the data protection review, and when asked what would take the time, my honest answer is mostly that same review.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: What a missed call is worth to us (average booking value or room revenue per call), what we already use to cover overflow and after-hours calls, whether it connects to our PMS or central reservation system, and whether the works council (Betriebsrat) would need to approve AI handling of recorded guest calls.

screens.why1: Right after the cost of the missed calls and who decides, asking what I'd charge the revenue director is the obvious next step.

screens.why3: It asks my own price, which I know: €3,000 up front from my partnership terms, and the per-hotel licence I have in mind.
screens.why4: The shapes are distinct and cover how I would charge; leaving out a percent is right, because my cost is 5% of calls rather than money; 'Free to them' is fair because the director, not the agent, pays; 'No price yet' is the right escape.
screens.why5: The belief keeps €3,000 up front and €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month, but my €3,000 is a money-back pilot at one hotel that is credited on roll-out, and 'up front' alone reads like a set-up fee I never charge.
screens.why7: The shapes follow the card (per-hotel unit and month locked from the cost, no percent of a non-money base, 'free to them' only offered where someone else decides). The belief keeps my whole range, unit and period with both steps, as one price first then a plan requires, and 'No price yet' is the only escape.
screens.instead: Same question and shapes; belief: Hotel group revenue directors would think Codyco worth €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel, then €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month.

screens.why1: Right after cost and price, asking who else has to sign off on a €3,000 pilot is the obvious next thing to settle for a hotel group sale.
screens.why2: Plain to me: 'revenue director', 'owner' and 'agree before they can buy' are how hotel group sales are talked about, though 'hotel group revenue director' reads a little stiff.
screens.why3: I know from my own pilots that the director decides and the hotel's owner, and often finance, have to agree, so I can answer this from what I see.
screens.why4: A free box with a clear limit (two roles, four words each), 'Nobody' allowed, and 'I'm not sure' as the only chip fits a founder who might not know yet.
screens.why5: My answer, the hotel's owner and the finance director, sits in the box as I typed it, and the director is named as the decider as I set it.
screens.why7: The box matches the card's founder role_list: at most two roles of up to four words in my order, 'Nobody' accepted for nobody_else, and 'I'm not sure' as the escape that leaves the dimension out.

screens.why1: Right after I named who has to agree, Keel shows me the list back to check, which is where it belongs.
screens.why2: Reservation agent, revenue director, hotel's owner and finance director are all plain words in a German hotel group, and the tags are simple.
screens.why3: Who signs off on a €3,000 pilot in a hotel group is something I deal with on every sales call.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct and tagged cleanly, but 'The finance director' is a role I never named, so the list is padded with one odd row.
screens.why5: I said the revenue or reservations director decides and the hotel's owner has to agree; the finance director has crept in even though the intro claims Keel used only my roles.
screens.why7: The shape holds (Nobody else first, the agent with the problem, the director deciding, at most two who agree, each tagged), but 'Keel adds none' is bent by a finance director I never named, and the belief would then test 'the owner and the finance director must agree'.
screens.instead: Nobody else · Reservation agent · has the problem · Hotel group revenue director · decides to buy · The hotel's owner · has to agree

screens.why1: After naming who decides and who else has to agree, choosing which of those beliefs to test is the obvious next step for me.
screens.why2: Revenue director, hotel's owner, finance director and sign off are plain words in a German hotel group's commercial side.
screens.why3: I know who has to agree before a hotel group pays a 3,000 euro pilot, since I sell to these directors every week.
screens.why4: The two roles are fused into one row, so I cannot test the owner alone, which is what I said; the card wants one row per role.
screens.why5: My answer was the hotel's owner, but the row and the bar add the finance director next to the owner, so it drifted a little from what I typed.
screens.why7: The card asks for one row per named role, and here two roles share a single row while the bar needs both to agree; Nobody else first, the tags, the belief's form and a bar that can hold or fail are all fine.
screens.instead: Which do you want to test? Nobody else / The hotel's owner (has to agree) / The finance director (has to agree), one row each, so I can test: The revenue director decides, and the hotel's owner must agree first.

screens.why1: Right after naming who else has to agree, asking what the hotel group has to clear before paying is the obvious next brake on the sale.
screens.why2: Short and plain; the hint's example and "not your own trial or pilot" make clear what is meant, though "the buyer's own side" is a bit generic where "the hotel group" would be my word.
screens.why3: I know what a German hotel group's legal and data protection people demand before guest calls go to an AI, so I can answer from my own sales calls.
screens.why4: The only chip is the escape "I'm not sure", which fits a box where I type the steps myself.
screens.why5: My step, "A data protection review of guest calls", stands in my own words, and nothing of my pilot or offer is pushed into it.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 buyer-side steps of at most 9 words, biggest first, excludes my own trial or pilot, leaves the time to me on the next screen and offers "I'm not sure" as the escape, all as the card requires.
screens.instead: What must the hotel group clear on its own side before it pays for Codyco (e.g. a data protection review, the works council)?

screens.why1: Right after I named who has to agree and before I pick a step and give its time, this is the obvious place to check the list of hurdles on the hotel group's side.
screens.why2: A data protection review and a works council sign-off (Betriebsrat) are everyday words to a German hotel group's revenue or reservations director; the intro's 'under 9 words' is a small wobble against 'at most 9'.
screens.why3: Both are hurdles I hear about on every sales call with German groups: the DSGVO review of guest card and personal data on recorded calls, and the Betriebsrat once an AI starts handling calls that staff used to take.
screens.why4: Two distinct steps with no overlap, my own biggest blocker first, and only one row added by Keel, clearly tagged.
screens.why5: My data protection review is kept word for word, and Keel's addition doesn't slip in my €3,000 pilot, money-back guarantee or anything else from my offer.
screens.why7: Both steps are brakes on the buyer's side that I don't control, and the one suggestion is the real gate the card itself names for this trade and place (a works council) rather than a formality or the purchase itself; the order, the count and Keel's single suggestion all meet the card, and a group without a Betriebsrat can still answer 'It wouldn't be needed', which counts for.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the steps the hotel group must clear, picking one to test and typing how long I expect it to take is the obvious next move before the price questions close out Step 4.
screens.why2: A data protection review of guest calls and a works council sign-off (Betriebsrat) are plain words to me selling to German hotel groups, and the intro and time box say clearly what to do.
screens.why3: I know from every pitch to a group's revenue director that the data protection officer looks at an AI taking guests' card and personal details, and I can put a number of weeks on it from my pilots.
screens.why4: Two distinct steps on the buyer's side, my own first and Keel's works council as a real German gate rather than a formality; 'I'm not sure' is the right escape for my own estimate; the only blemish is the same hint printed twice on the screen.
screens.why5: The data protection review is my row in my words, the 4 weeks in the belief is the time I typed, and nothing of my pilot or pitch is posing as a step.
screens.why7: The measure is the step's own time, my typed 4 weeks is the edge, the bar counts under 4 weeks and not needed as for (so the 4-weeks-and-up bands go against and the belief can fall either way), Keel added only one real buyer-side gate, and the founder's escape is there.

screens.why1: Right after the buyer, the sign-offs and the time to clear them, asking what first step the revenue director would take before paying is the natural close of the commercial part, and my pilot is exactly that step.
screens.why2: Plain to me on first read; 'pilot', 'trial' and 'pay for' are how I sell to hotel groups, and the 9-word limit and the money/data/signature note are clear.
screens.why3: It asks about my own offer, which I know cold: €3,000 up front, money back, one location.
screens.why4: A box to type in with the single 'I'm not sure' chip, which the card allows on the founder's side, so it fits.
screens.why5: My answer 'pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel' sits whole inside the 9 words, keeping the euro amount, money-back and one hotel, so nothing of mine has to be cut.
screens.why7: The box asks for what the card's step needs: one step, at most 9 words, taken by the decider, saying where the money goes, with the smaller free step promised on the next screen because mine costs money; the escape is the founder's allowed 'I'm not sure'.

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first step and its cost, Keel shows how strangers will hear it and what the soft yes will be, which is the obvious next check before the commercial part closes.
screens.why2: My step and the four answers read cleanly, but the smaller-step line itself reads 'Yes, after see a demo on sample calls first', which is ungrammatical and made me read it twice to see what Keel had stored.
screens.why3: Whether a revenue director would pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel is exactly the call I put to hotel groups every week, and they know their own answer.
screens.why4: There is a firm yes to my step, a soft yes after a free demo, probably not, and no; they are distinct and complete, and no escape is needed because No is the floor.
screens.why5: €3,000, money-back, pilot and one hotel are all my own terms, kept within nine words, and a free demo on sample calls is close to the free test number we offer anyway.
screens.why7: The served list meets the card (the step whole after 'Yes, I'd', the soft yes in the -ing form on a free smaller step because the step costs money, two answers for and two against, no escape), but the stored smaller step is the verb phrase 'see a demo on sample calls' rather than the noun phrase the card asks for, and that is why the founder's row prints ungrammatically.
screens.instead: Your step, as strangers hear it: pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel · Or a smaller step first: a demo on sample calls · Yes, I'd pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel / Probably, after seeing a demo on sample calls first / Probably not / No

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious moment to decide whether to collect pilot leads, after I have just set my commitment step on screens 20 and 21.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' with 'Yes, ask them' or 'No pilot' reads plainly on the first pass, and the hint says exactly what strangers will see and where I will find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads is my own call, and I run a pilot offer already, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: My pilot is 'pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel', but the line strangers get is a free 'Leave your email', so 'pilot' here drifts from what I typed; it also doesn't say whether reservation agents, who cannot sign a pilot, get the line or only the revenue directors.
screens.instead: Offer your pilot to the revenue directors who answer? They'll see: "Would you try Codyco at one hotel, €3,000, money back if it doesn't pay off? Leave your email." -- Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is an obvious last step before the link goes out to reservation agents, and it was not asked earlier.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, voice, typing, credits and text message into one paragraph, and it says 'voice' while the recorded pick says 'face', so I would read it twice to know what I'm locking.
screens.why3: Picking the interviewer for my own study after hearing two 5-second samples is something I can do right now.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a sample, a preselected default and the same cost either way; no escape is needed for a pick like this.
screens.why5: The screen only names my respondents, reservation agents, and adds nothing of Codyco's product or roles that would leak to them.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, and in which language: German or English? (Daphne / Saskia, each with a 5 s sample; same 400 credits either way)

screens.why1: The study goes out on two links, one to reservation agents (screen 23) and one to the revenue directors who decide, so asking how the directors' link should run belongs right here, just before sending.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, let them choose: each option is plain, and each says in one line what the director would see.
screens.why3: I know my buyers: hotel group revenue directors are busy and spend their days at a screen, so I can judge whether they would sit through a video or would rather tap through between meetings.
screens.why4: The three options cover every format (voice, text, or the respondent's pick), they don't overlap, and my pick, Read and tap, is there.
screens.why5: "Directors" cuts my "hotel group revenue director" to one word; it's clear in this flow but loses the revenue and hotel group part I typed.
screens.instead: How should hotel group revenue directors answer? (AI interviewer Daphne / Read and tap / Let them choose)

screens.why1: After choosing how directors answer, asking who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending, and I as founder with 7 hotel groups know my directors by name.
screens.why2: The three choices are plain to me as a founder: named people, a Keel contact list, or one open link posted where people are.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would send this to — the revenue and reservations directors at the groups I already talk to — so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete, but the middle one leans on 'the Contacts page', a Keel screen I haven't seen in this flow, so it needs a second read.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product, my roles or my numbers is touched or leaked here; it is purely about distribution.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- Directors I know by name (one link each) / A list I search for in Keel (one link each, I send them) / One open link I post where directors already are (each signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits under the title with the deciding card and its number, 'Purchase friction: 4 of 8 under 4 weeks or not needed', and the card itself shows that 4 of 8 is 2 short of the 6-of-8 bar.
screens.why_b2: Most cards show who was counted and where the bar sits. But I had to look twice at Ability to pay ('4 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed': 5 of what, when 8 answered?) and at the kicker's '4 TO 8 COUNTED'.
screens.why_b3: These are my six beliefs in my words: 5% of reservation calls ringing out, €3,000 up front then €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month, the data protection review of guest calls, and the money-back pilot at one hotel.
screens.why_b4: The only line under the verdict says who was asked, not what to do. Nothing tells me to, say, have a data-protection pack ready, or to lead with the pilot since 6 of 8 would pay for it.
screens.why_b5: Price at 4 of 8, 2 short, is called 'split', while Purchase friction at the same 4 of 8, 2 short, is 'Did not hold'. That makes the deciding card look harsher than its twin, and the page never says that 8 directors is a small base.
screens.instead: Did not hold on one card: only 4 of 8 directors expect the data protection review of guest calls to clear within 4 weeks (most say 4 weeks to 3 months), even though 6 of 8 would pay €3,000 for the money-back pilot. Bring a ready DPA and a call-recording data sheet to every pilot pitch, and plan for a 1 to 3 month close. A small sample of 8.

screens.why_b1: The status says People disagree and puts 4 of 7 at 5% or more against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short, right beside it, so I know my 5% did not clear the bar, though the doubled 'People disagree a split' reads clumsily.
screens.why_b2: The axis is % of the reservation calls a month, there are 7 cells for 7 counted, and my marker sits at 5 with the bar at 5 of 7, all plain on first look, even if the two fives sit close together.
screens.why_b3: Existing sacrifice at about 5% of the reservation calls per hotel a month, from booking calls that rang out unanswered, is my own number and my own loss line, even though the line no longer says hotel groups.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and sends me to the Price card; it never says what the split means for my 5% claim, for instance that the three short of it are at 4%, 2% and none.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called a lean and not a call, Hannes's none is shown as counted as 0, and Karim is set apart, so nothing claims more than seven directors can carry.
screens.instead: Half the directors see 5% or more, up to 10% at resort hotels; the three below are at 4%, 2% (a call center covers after hours) and none, so lead with the 5% for groups without after-hours cover, and ask more directors before putting it in the pitch.

screens.why_b1: The deciding number is there and tied to the bar (4 of 8, bar 6 of 8, 2 short), but the status says 'People disagree, a split' rather than that my price did not hold, though 2 short of a 2-in-3 bar is a miss.
screens.why_b2: The up-front chart reads cleanly with my €3,000 on a band edge and the 6-of-8 marker, but the monthly chart and its strip count only 7 (Hannes's would-not-pay shows as 0 there, though the rule counts him against on both), so I had to look twice to make 8 answered agree with 4 for and 3 against.
screens.why_b3: It's my €3,000 up front then €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month, but it drops that the €3,000 is a money-back pilot at one hotel credited on roll-out, and 'per hotel, once' reads like €3,000 for each hotel in the group.
screens.why_b4: The So line only points me to the Insights tab, though the quotes on this very card say what to do: show missed bookings on the group's own numbers, offer a free test number, and make the licence pay off at a 4% miss rate across nine hotels.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is honest, but the monthly strip leaves out one person who counts against, which understates the opposition on the licence.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 8 would pay €3,000 up front and €1,000 a month, 2 short of 6; Hannes is against on both parts, so the licence is 4 for and 4 against. The 4 below want proof on their own call data or a free month first, so lead with the money-back pilot and show the payback per hotel.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', and the So line repeats it, so I know the belief is undecided because only 4 directors reached my €3,000 / €1,000 and the floor is 5.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count where the money would come from over the 4 asked, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a ghost cell, when only 4 were asked, takes a second look to read as 'the floor is 5 and 2 in 3 of 5 means 4'.
screens.why_b3: The belief line carries my own numbers (€3,000 up front, then €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month) and my buyer, but it is a sentence Keel derived and I never checked, shown as 'Your belief' as though I had typed it.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until 5 have' tells me I need one more director at my price, but it does not say what the lean means for selling the pilot: 3 of the 4 who would pay would use a line they already have, with only Roberto needing a new one.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and 'a lean, not a call' is said honestly, but the rule line misstates the chart: it omits 'charged to the teams or sites' as for and 'grant or outside funding' as against, and names an against answer, 'or none', that is not among the options.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only 4 of 8 directors named €3,000 up front and €1,000 a month or more; 3 of those 4 would pay from a budget line they already have, 1 would need a new line. That leans your way, so reach one more director at your price to make the call. Counts for you: an existing line, charged to the sites that use it, or other spending; against: a new line or outside funding.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 6 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, marked "at the bar", so I know it held, and only just.
screens.why_b2: The four answers carry their counts and for/against tags, the strip shows 6 for and 2 against over 8 people, and the marker sits at 6, so the chart reads in one look.
screens.why_b3: My belief was that the revenue director decides and the hotel's owner has to agree, but the line adds a finance director I never put forward, though the dimension name and the owner are mine.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for the hotel's owner in most deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone" tells me concretely to bring the owner into the €3,000 pilot pitch.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the count line says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and a result exactly at the bar is called holding up, not strong.
screens.instead: The hotel group revenue director decides, and the hotel's owner must agree first. Holding up at the bar, 6 of 8, so plan for the owner in most deals.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits beside 4 of 8 under 4 weeks or not needed, against a bar of 6 of 8, 2 short, so I know the verdict and the number behind it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the 8 directors' bands, each marked for or against, and the strip puts the marker at 6, so I can see where the bar is and how far short 4 falls.
screens.why_b3: It is my step, a data protection review of guest calls, and my 4 weeks, asked of the revenue directors who decide.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a review cycle of 4 weeks to 3 months rather than my 4 weeks, and points me to the Insights tab for what takes the time, which I can act on in the pilot timeline.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible and the count line says it is a lean, not a call; the chart also says my 4 weeks is the low edge of the band counted against, so "longer than your 4 weeks" isn't hidden.
screens.instead: Say "4 of 8 expect 4 weeks or more" rather than "longer than your 4 weeks", since the band they picked starts at my exact time.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits next to "6 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the count that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts answers to the pilot question over the 8 directors, and the strip shows 6 for, 2 against with the marker at the bar of 6, all clear on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is Commitment and the belief is my own step word for word (pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel), with the revenue director as the one who decides, as I set it up.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" tells me plainly to take the six yeses straight to the paid pilot.
screens.why_b5: The count line does call it a lean, but the So line says "book them into it" without saying it sits exactly on the bar (one more no and it fails) or that only 4 of 8 put €3,000 or more on the Price card, which is the same fee, so it reads firmer than 8 answers can carry.
screens.instead: Holding up, only just: 6 of 8 would pay €3,000 for the money-back pilot, exactly at the bar, so one more no would sink it. Only 4 of 8 named €3,000 or more on Price, so book the six but confirm the fee with each on the call. (And fix the rule line's "after see a demo" to "after seeing a demo".)

screens.why_b1: Every box opens on its verdict word with the deciding count beside it: Price 4 of 8 against a bar of 6, Purchase friction 4 of 8 with 2 short, Buyer and payer 6 of 8 at the bar.
screens.why_b3: Price and Purchase friction are my beliefs in my words, but the Buyer and payer line adds a finance director I never named; I said the director decides and the owner has to agree.
screens.why_b4: Under 'When a line fails' nothing says what the result means; the quotes hint at moves (prove the missed bookings on their own phone report, a free test number, licence economics for a nine-hotel group), but the screen never draws them.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the at-the-bar hold isn't called strong, but Price 2 short is softened to 'People disagree', and Buyer and payer promises 'the 2 who said no' then shows one quote that reads as an easy yes ('he'd agree quickly').
screens.why_b6: The Price quotes teach me things I did not type: at 4% a €1,000 licence across nine hotels costs more than it recovers, groups with call centers want the loss shown on their own numbers before paying, and one director won't risk reputation on an AI at any price; the empty Purchase friction box adds nothing.
screens.instead: Price missed by 2 of 8: the doubters want proof of lost calls on their own phone report and a price that scales below €1,000 per hotel for big groups, so lead with a free missed-call audit and a group rate; Purchase friction failed but nobody was asked why, so ask the 4 what the data protection review involves.

screens.why1: On the buying-decision link, the idea card has to come first, before I'm asked anything about it, so it is obviously in the right place.
screens.why2: Missed booking calls, payment, the PMS and handing calls to the reservations desk are all my everyday words, though "in each hotel's voice" took a moment to place.
screens.why3: Unanswered calls after hours, at peak and on holidays in our central reservations office are exactly what I deal with and pay for, so I can judge this from my own work.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options, rows or chips.
screens.why5: It names what the tool does and how, in hotel terms, with no internal labels or founder jargon reaching me; the belief only restates the first line rather than adding to it.
screens.why6: Heard once, "calls nobody picks up" comes three times in six sentences and the second sentence repeats the first, so it drags; PMS is fine said aloud in my trade.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that takes the calls nobody picks up. Your hotels forward unanswered calls to it; it answers in each hotel's name, takes the payment and writes the booking straight into your PMS, and passes a call to your desk by rules you set. The people building it believe this would turn those missed calls into bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what share of booking calls my reservations office failed to answer last month is the obvious first cost question for someone who pays for call handling.
screens.why2: "Go without in booking calls that rang out unanswered" is a tangled phrase; I'd say "what percent of reservation calls went unanswered" and had to read it twice to see it means the same thing.
screens.why3: I know our abandoned and unanswered call rate from the ACD reports; I quote it as 6% myself, so I can answer from what I see every week.
screens.why4: The percent box is right for the measure, but serving both a None chip and I can't recall gives two ways to say nothing, and None as 0% of calls is slightly odd beside a percent box.
screens.why5: The founder's base "the reservation calls" and the rate mode are kept, but "go without" is the card's forbidden lose-word in disguise, and the clause drifts from the plain loss line of calls that ring out unanswered.
screens.why6: Heard once, "did you go without in booking calls that rang out unanswered" is a mouthful and the spoken label repeats the stem, though it is one question with one escape said last.
screens.why7: The measure is the founder's percent of the reservation calls over a month, so for and against both stay open and the escape is there, but the item uses "go without", which the card forbids where a plain verb can be said.
screens.instead: Last month, about what percent of your reservation calls rang out unanswered? [box] % of reservation calls last month · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about unanswered calls, asking what it would be worth to us is exactly the next thing I'd expect as the one who pays for booking tools.
screens.why2: Up front, per hotel and a month per hotel is how setup fees and per-property subscriptions are quoted to me, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I sign off on setup fees and monthly per-property charges for reservations and channel tools all the time, so I can place this against what I already pay.
screens.why4: Both ladders are complete, distinct and non-overlapping, use plain euro amounts, and end with I wouldn't pay for this, with I can't say set apart as the escape.
screens.why5: The product shows only through the deliberate idea card, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Each step reads four short options and then one escape, and the two-band follow-up is easy to hold when heard, so I can answer both the one-off and the monthly price by ear.
screens.why7: Each ladder is on one measure (euros per hotel, up front and then a month), with six rungs and a clear edge where bands from the founder's price up can support the belief and the lower bands plus I wouldn't pay can refute it, and the single escape is I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I gave a price for Codyco, asking where that money would come from is the obvious next question for the person who signs off on reservation tools.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off and other spending are how I talk about money every year in planning, though the stem drops the 'per hotel' the price screen had, so I'd assume it still means per hotel.
screens.why3: I own the reservations and revenue budget for the group, so I know exactly which pot this would come out of.
screens.why4: My true answer is there (taken from other spending, meaning the after-hours call-center contract we already pay), but 'a grant or outside funding' is an odd option for a hotel group buying a booking tool.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or terms leaks; 'teams or sites' reads naturally to me as departments or hotels.
screens.why6: Heard once it's a short single question with five short sources read as a list and one escape, easy to hold and answer.
screens.why7: Five sources of money in the card's order with three for and two against, the escape 'I can't say' set apart, and the stem points back to my own price as the chain requires.
screens.instead: You said about €3,000 to €5,000 up front per hotel, then €1,000 to €2,500 a month. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? (same five options, I can't say)

screens.why1: Straight after where the money would come from, asking who has to agree to spend it is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Sign off" and "the hotel's owner" are words I use every day, and the question reads once and is clear.
screens.why3: I know who approves spend in our group, but in a group with a central reservations office the per-hotel owner is often not the one who agrees (our Geschäftsführung is), so I'd half-guess how 'the hotel's owner' maps onto us.
screens.why4: The four run from me alone to someone else's call, each is distinct, and 'I can't say' fits as the one escape.
screens.why5: The owner as the one who must agree comes through as a plain role with no product talk leaking.
screens.why6: One short either-or question, the price says well aloud, and the four options and the escape are easy to hold.
screens.why7: The measure is one (who must agree), the four come in the card's order with the tested role in the second, the belief can be supported or refuted, and 'I can't say' is the required escape, kept apart.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about €3,000 per hotel yourself, or would the owner or management company have to agree? I could sign off myself · The owner would have to agree · Several people would have to agree · It's someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, asking how long our own data protection check on recording guest calls would hold the purchase up is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: A data protection review is everyday language for anyone buying tools in a German hotel group, since every new system that touches guest data goes past our Datenschutzbeauftragter.
screens.why3: I have taken tools through our data protection officer before, so I know roughly how long a review of anything that records or processes guest calls takes.
screens.why4: The bands are clean and don't overlap, they run from quick to very long, 'It wouldn't be needed' covers the case where no review is required, and 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the name already shown on the idea card, and the step is phrased the way my side would put it, not as a sales term.
screens.why6: It is one short question, the first step reads four options I can hold, and the second step is a simple either-or.
screens.why7: Every option measures the step's own duration, the 4-week edge sits exactly at the founder's time with two bands plus 'not needed' for and three bands against, the step is a real brake on the buyer's side, and 'I can't tell' is the only escape.

screens.why1: The follow-up belongs after the duration question, but I was just asked about the data protection review specifically, so asking broadly what would take the time in buying Codyco feels like it half-asks what I already named.
screens.why2: It's plain, and 'you said 4 weeks to 3 months' reads back my pick the way I'd say it, so I know at once what it refers to.
screens.why3: I know exactly what drags: our data protection officer, the works council because calls get recorded and agents get monitored, and a processing agreement with the vendor.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: Codyco is the name from the idea card I was shown, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said 4 weeks to 3 months for the data protection review. What would take that long?

screens.why1: After price, budget, sign-off and the data protection review, asking whether I would actually put money down for a pilot is the obvious last question of the buying part.
screens.why2: A €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel is how vendors pitch to me, and I read it once and know exactly what I'm agreeing to.
screens.why3: I decide and pay for booking tools at our group, so whether I'd fund a pilot at one property is my own call.
screens.why4: Firm yes, yes after a demo on sample calls, probably not and no cover how I would really respond, and none of them overlap.
screens.why5: The €3,000, the money back and the one hotel are all kept, and nothing reaches me that I wasn't meant to see beyond the idea card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: Heard once it is one question with four short answers; the first is long but just repeats the question, so it is easy to hold.
screens.why7: The first yes names the founder's paid, money-back step whole, the soft yes puts a free demo on sample calls before it (no money, data or signature), then probably not and no with no escape: two for, two against.
